title: Food and hosting
verifiedBy: Claude Opus 5 — LLM review, authorised by repo owner

rules.text: para names who something is for: para mí, para ti. It is the only job para does in this level — the por/para contrast is a whole system and waits.
mí with an accent is "me" after a preposition; mi without one is "my". Para mi and para mí are two different sentences, and only the accent tells them apart.
An object pronoun goes BEFORE the conjugated verb: lo quiero, me pone. English puts the object after the verb and Spanish never does.
otro never takes an article. Un otro café is the English "another" translated word for word, and it is wrong: ¿Quieres otro café?
que joins a verb of thinking or saying to what follows it, and it cannot be dropped: creo que está frío. English leaves "that" out all the time and Spanish never does.
Hunger and thirst are things you HAVE in Spanish: tengo hambre, tengo sed. Estoy hambre is not a sentence, and it is what English produces.

sentences.display: Para mí, una sopa, por favor.

words.note: Names the person something is for. That is the only job it does in this level; the por/para contrast is a system and it waits for later.
The shape "me" takes after a preposition, and the accent is what separates it from mi, "my". ti is the same for someone you call tú, and it takes no accent at all.

sentences.trap: No verb anywhere. Spanish orders by naming who it is for and what it is, and adding a verb makes it sound like a report.
sentences.sound: MI, one clean syllable, and the accent marks meaning rather than stress here.

variations.display: Para mí, un café, por favor.
variations.changed: a different order in the same frame
ti, which carries no accent
no article at all, because it is not being counted

mistake.why: Without the accent mi means "my", so the sentence reads "for my". The accent is not decoration.

sentences.usage: How a table orders. The waiter goes round and each person says their para mí.
sentences.mnemonic: The accent turns my into me.

sentences.cue: Could I have a coffee, please?

words.note: poner, to put. At a bar it means to pour or serve, and ¿Me pone…? is what people actually say in Spain where a book would offer ¿Me da…?

sentences.trap: The verb means "put". Nothing in the sentence says "have" or "could", and the frame carries all of it.
sentences.sound: PO-ne. The n is fully said and the final e never falls silent.

variations.changed: a number, and the noun goes plural

variations.cue: Could I have a little milk?
variations.changed: un poco de measuring instead of counting

variations.cue: Can you get me a coffee?
variations.changed: the tú form, to someone you know

mistake.why: me goes in front of the conjugated verb: ¿Me pone…? It never follows one.

sentences.usage: A bar in Spain. In Latin America ¿Me da…? or ¿Me trae…? is commoner, and both are understood everywhere.
sentences.mnemonic: At a bar they do not give you a coffee, they put you one.

sentences.cue: The bread? I want it warm.

words.note: Stands for a masculine thing already named, and it goes in FRONT of the verb: lo quiero. The feminine and plural forms are spelled like the articles, so this course teaches the rule on lo alone.

sentences.trap: lo quiero, not quiero lo. The pronoun climbs in front of the verb and stays there.
sentences.sound: The two words run together — lo-KYE-ro — with no pause between them.

variations.cue: The coffee? I want it very hot.
variations.changed: another masculine thing, and muy in front

variations.cue: The bread? I don't want it.
variations.changed: no in front of everything, including the pronoun
asked as a question, in the tú form

mistake.why: The pronoun goes before the verb: lo quiero caliente.

sentences.usage: Answering a question about something already on the table. Naming the thing again would be heavy.
sentences.mnemonic: The little word runs ahead of the verb.

words.note: Never takes an article. Un otro café is English translated word for word and it is wrong; otro already carries the "an".

sentences.trap: English needs "an" inside "another" and Spanish forbids it. This is the whole lesson of the sentence.
sentences.sound: O-tro, two beats, with the tr said as one quick tap.

variations.changed: feminine, so the word ends in -a
the usted form, at a table you do not know

variations.cue: No thanks, I don't want another.
variations.changed: otro standing alone, with the noun left out

mistake.why: otro takes no article: otro café. The un is already inside it.

sentences.usage: The offer a host makes, and it is made more than once. See S05 for what a refusal has to do.
sentences.mnemonic: otro is already "an other" — do not buy the an twice.

sentences.display: No, gracias, no tengo mucha hambre.
sentences.cue: No thanks, I'm not very hungry.
sentences.literal: No, thanks, not I-have much hunger.

words.note: M1's mucho counting a feminine noun, so it agrees: mucha hambre, mucha agua. Its row is L1-M1's; this is the shape that row never showed.
A noun, so Spanish HAS it: tengo hambre. Feminine, but it takes el in the singular like el agua, because it starts with a stressed a.

sentences.trap: estoy hambre is not a sentence in any dialect. Hunger, thirst, cold and fear are all things you have.
sentences.sound: AM-bre. The h is silent, as it is in every Spanish word.

variations.changed: the flat refusal, without mucha
both nouns on one tengo
the question, and still with tener

mistake.why: hambre is a noun and estar cannot take one. It is tengo hambre.

sentences.usage: A refusal that lands. A bare No, gracias will be heard as politeness and the offer will come again.
sentences.mnemonic: You do not BE hungry in Spanish; you HAVE hunger.

sentences.display: Creo que la sopa está fría.
sentences.cue: I think the soup is cold.
sentences.literal: I-think that the soup is cold.

words.note: creer, to think or believe. Softer than pienso for an opinion about a fact, and it is what people reach for first.
Joins the thinking to what is thought, and it is never dropped: creo QUE está fría. It carries no accent — M4's qué, which asks, does.

sentences.trap: English drops "that" so often it feels optional. In Spanish leaving que out is not a style choice; the sentence breaks.
sentences.sound: KE, one syllable, with a plain k — the u in que is never said.

variations.display: Creo que el café está frío.
variations.cue: I think the coffee is cold.
variations.changed: a masculine thing, so the adjective moves
ser, because it is a quality and not a state
the negative, which in careful Spanish would go further still

mistake.why: que is obligatory after a verb of thinking: creo que la sopa está fría.

sentences.usage: How a complaint starts at a table — softly, and about the food rather than the person.
sentences.mnemonic: Spanish never leaves the that out.

sentences.cue: Could I have the bill, please?

words.note: traer, to bring. ¿Me trae…? is the standard way to ask for anything to be brought to a table, everywhere Spanish is spoken.
Feminine: la cuenta. In Latin America you will also hear la nota; la cuenta is understood everywhere.

sentences.trap: la cuenta, with the article. Asking for cuenta with nothing in front of it sounds like an accounting term.
sentences.sound: TRA-e is two syllables, not one. KWEN-ta, with the ue gliding as always.

variations.cue: Could you bring me a glass of water?
variations.changed: something else brought to the table

variations.cue: Could you bring me another coffee, please?
variations.changed: otro from S04, in this frame
the shortest it gets, and perfectly polite

mistake.why: me goes in front: ¿Me trae la cuenta? The pronoun never follows a conjugated verb.

sentences.usage: The last sentence of a meal. In Spain you have to ask; the bill will not arrive by itself.
sentences.mnemonic: Nothing comes to a Spanish table until you ask for it.

sentences.display: Tengo sed, ¿me da un vaso de agua?
sentences.cue: I'm thirsty, could I have a glass of water?
sentences.literal: I-have thirst, to-me give(polite) a glass of water?

words.note: A noun, like hambre, and you HAVE it: tengo sed. Feminine: la sed.

sentences.trap: Two clauses and no "and" between them. Spanish is happy to let a comma carry the join here.
sentences.sound: SED, one syllable, and the final d is barely there — softer than an English d.

variations.cue: I'm thirsty, could I have a water?
variations.changed: M5's own verb instead of dar
the question, in the tú form
the refusal that names its reason

mistake.why: sed is a noun, so it goes with tener: tengo sed.

sentences.usage: Everyday. Naming the reason before the request is what makes it warm rather than abrupt.
sentences.mnemonic: Hunger and thirst are both things you carry.

sentences.display: Quiero carne y verdura, por favor.
sentences.cue: I'd like meat and vegetables, please.

words.note: Feminine: la carne. Uncountable in Spanish as in English, so it takes no article when you are naming the kind.
Singular in Spanish where English is plural: la verdura is vegetables as a kind. verduras counts individual ones.

sentences.trap: verdura is singular. English speakers reach for the plural because their own word only exists in it.
sentences.sound: KAR-ne, with one tapped r. ver-DU-ra, with two.

variations.changed: one thing rather than two
the same order in S01's frame

variations.cue: I don't want meat, I want fish.
variations.changed: a refusal with an alternative

mistake.display: Quiero la carne y las verduras.
mistake.why: With the articles you are asking for particular ones you can see. To name the kind, leave them out.

sentences.usage: Ordering from a menu that offers a choice. The articles come back when you point at something.
sentences.mnemonic: Name a kind and drop the article.

words.note: Fish as food. A fish still swimming is a pez, and the two are different words — the one on the plate has been caught.

sentences.trap: el pescado, with the article, even though English says just "fish". gustar always takes one in front of the thing liked.
sentences.sound: pes-KA-do, and the d between vowels is the soft th of "this".

variations.changed: a feminine noun, so the article moves
the answer, with mucho on the verb
the negative, with no in front of everything

mistake.why: gustar needs the article: ¿Te gusta el pescado? Leaving it out is the English shape.

sentences.usage: What a host asks before deciding what to cook. The answer is expected to be honest.
sentences.mnemonic: gustar always brings the article with it.
